description: We’re Rishabh and Neil, computer science students at the University of Maryland who share a love of space exploration. We enjoy turning complex data into tools people can use, and we’re excited to use NASA’s open data to build something that makes space more accessible and inspiring for everyone.
summary:
Lunar Transit is a free browser game where players design a space mission and fly it from Earth to the Moon. With a fixed budget of 1,000 credits, players choose from 12 spacecraft parts across shielding, propulsion and instruments. Every part has a cost, a mass and a power draw: heavier ships fly slower, power is capped, and unspent credits become fuel for abilities and repairs during flight. In a three-minute live flight, six telegraphed hazards such as solar flares and orbital debris test the design. On arrival, players complete one of five hands-on lunar science tasks, and a mission report shows exactly how each decision affected the outcome. We designed it around what makes games engaging: competition and seeing your decisions play out in real time.

The game answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning engineering trade-offs that are usually taught in theory into decisions players make, test and learn from in minutes. It supports solo play with personal bests, online one-versus-one, and two-player co-op with distinct Pilot and Engineer roles. Educational content drawn from NASA resources, including CubeSat 101, GMAT and Goddard's Mission Design Lab, appears throughout. It runs in any browser with no download: https://lunar-transit.onrender.com
details:
What it does and how it works

Lunar Transit is a complete space mission in a browser, in five stages:

  1. Design: spend up to 1,000 credits choosing from 12 attachments and an optional Repair Drone. You can’t afford everything, and mass and power are limited, so every pick is a trade-off.
  2. Launch: the ship flies an Earth-to-Moon trajectory automatically; its speed depends on thrust versus mass.
  3. Survive the flight: six hazards, like solar flares and orbital debris, arrive with warnings. Players respond with five boosters and protectors, plus repairs with the Repair Drone, all costing credits and limited by cooldowns. In 1v1, five deterrents can also slow down the opponent. After three minutes comes a one-minute overtime at half cost and half effect, then autopilot brings any surviving ship to the Moon. However, oftentimes players don't reach overtime.
  4. Do the science: solve one of five lunar tasks, such as analyzing surface spectra, pointing an antenna at Earth, or planning orbit burns.
  5. The goal: finish the whole mission, from launch to completed science task, as fast as possible. Solo players and Co-op crews race their personal best; in 1v1, the first player to survive the flight and do the science wins. A mission report shows how each decision affected the result.

Modes: Solo and Co-op with Easy, Normal and Hard difficulty and saved personal bests; online 1v1 by private room code or quick match, where both players get identical starter ships and the identical science task; two-player co-op with a shared ship and budget, where the Pilot controls speed and the Engineer controls shields and repairs; and a guided 60-second tutorial offered automatically to first-time visitors.

Why we built it this way

Engagement shaped this project from the start. Looking back at the games we enjoy most, two things kept them compelling: competition, and seeing our decisions play out in real time. So we built Lunar Transit around both. Instead of designing a spacecraft and waiting for a score, players watch their build fly live: a heavy shield visibly slows the ship, a solar flare hits and the hull holds or doesn’t, a thruster burn changes the race immediately. Online 1v1 adds a rival flying the identical route and racing to solve the identical science task, with deterrents like jammers and EMPs to raise the stakes. Co-op brings the same real-time pressure to a two-person crew. Our goal was that players learn mission-design trade-offs because they feel the consequences, and come back to try a better build.

Benefits and intended impact

Most learning tools teach orbits, rockets or subsystems one at a time. Lunar Transit makes system-level trade-offs tangible. Shielding adds protection but also mass, so the ship is slower and meets more hazards. Engines add speed but draw power. Saving credits buys flexibility mid-flight. Because there is no single winning build, players experiment, fail, redesign and try again. Short sessions, plain-language explanations, a tutorial and immediate feedback make it suitable for classrooms, clubs and outreach.

NASA grounding

The game includes 32 short facts, each citing a NASA resource (CubeSat 101, GMAT, JPL Concept Maturity Levels, Goddard’s Mission Design Lab and others), shown during launch and on the results screen. Every part in the shop has a “The real science” panel explaining the real engineering principle and what the game simplifies. During each lunar task, the science behind it stays on screen beside the task along with its NASA sources. Game-balance numbers are clearly labelled as not being NASA data, and all content is bundled so the game needs no live NASA service.

Tools and technologies

TypeScript throughout. React and Vite for the interface; Three.js via React Three Fiber for procedurally drawn 3D visuals, with no image assets; Zustand for state. Node.js and Socket.IO run a server-authoritative multiplayer server with a fixed 20 Hz simulation. Zod validates every player command, and Vitest runs 69 automated tests covering the economy, movement, abilities, hazards, phases, tasks, victory rules and multiplayer. Hosted on Render; source on GitHub: https://github.com/Rishabh-and-Neil/lunar-transit. SI tools (Anthropic’s Claude) assisted with code, debugging, troubleshooting, and text.

What makes it creative

One deterministic rules engine powers solo play in the browser, the multiplayer server and the autopilot, so every mode plays by exactly the same physics. Every mission ends with real science rather than a simple finish line, and the mission report turns each run into a lesson for the next build.

Factors we considered

  • Fairness and anti-cheating: the server validates every action; a player who leaves cancels the match rather than handing a free win.
  • Accessibility: tutorial, difficulty levels, and mouse, touch and keyboard controls.
  • Reliability: bundled offline content, plus a reconnect grace period for dropped connections.
  • Honesty: clear separation of NASA facts from gameplay values, with SI use disclosed.
  • Current scope: a fixed translunar route rather than a launch-vehicle or orbit picker, and two players per online match.
